analysis.one_liner: Caps Medicare drug copays at the drug's actual net price after manufacturer rebates.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with support from one Democrat and one Republican but never received a committee hearing or vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When a Medicare Part D plan sets what a senior pays at the pharmacy counter, it bases that copay on the drug's list price — even though the plan gets big rebates back from the manufacturer and actually pays much less. This bill would cap a senior's cost-sharing at that lower, true net price, and let the government fine plans that charge more. It never got a hearing in the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D enrollees, especially seniors taking brand-name drugs with large manufacturer rebates. Today their copays can be set off a price well above what the plan really pays after rebates; this bill would require cost-sharing to reflect the net price instead, cutting what seniors pay at the pharmacy [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Beginning in plan year 2026, a beneficiary's cost-sharing for a covered Part D drug could not exceed the drug's negotiated price net of manufacturer price concessions [S2][S3].
Plans that violate the cap could face civil monetary penalties determined by the Secretary of Health and Human Services [S2][S3].
Copayments for low-income beneficiaries would likewise be capped at the net price, extending the same protection to seniors on subsidy programs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and the insurers that sponsor Part D plans, which currently keep some of the difference between a drug's list-based cost-sharing and the lower net price after rebates. Some plans could try to recover that revenue through higher premiums for all enrollees [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug middlemen and Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: Plans and pharmacy benefit managers would lose rebate-derived revenue that is now built into beneficiary cost-sharing, and a plausible way to recover it is higher premiums spread across all Part D enrollees, meaning some seniors could pay more monthly than they save per prescription [S2][S3].
The cap is keyed to the previous year's Detailed DIR Report of manufacturer price concessions, so it could lag price changes and depend on reporting data that plans control [S3].

The bill leaves the rebate system itself untouched: manufacturers would keep paying large back-end rebates rather than lowering listed prices, so the underlying pricing structure stays in place [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and easy to see: lower out-of-pocket drug costs for millions of Medicare enrollees at the pharmacy counter. The main cost is that plans might shift lost rebate revenue into premiums, which could modestly offset savings for some enrollees and raise costs for seniors on cheaper drugs. On balance the bill targets a real gap between what seniors are charged and what their plans actually pay, and it includes penalties to make the cap enforceable.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until the 118th Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Casey (D-PA) and Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) introduced the bill on July 20, 2023 [S3][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S1][S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history; it was never reported out of committee or brought to the floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D plan sponsors keep the margin between list-based copays and the net prices they actually pay, and manufacturers keep the rebate-driven pricing system untouched.

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey, Jr.
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap Part D cost-sharing at the net price of a drug

for.name: Sen. John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's cosponsor, making the bill bipartisan from introduction

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it without a path to the floor

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship from one Democrat and one Republican, but no vote ever occurred, so the chamber's party split on it was never tested.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D plan sponsors
industries.note: These middlemen currently base beneficiary copays on prices above what they actually pay after manufacturer rebates. The bill would cap cost-sharing at the net price and penalize plans that exceed it, cutting into that spread [S2][S3].

The bill leaves the rebate system fully intact: manufacturers would keep paying large back-end concessions to keep their drugs on formularies instead of lowering list prices. It redirects some of that rebate value to seniors' copays but does not reform the pricing structure itself [S2][S3].
Insurers offering Part D plans would face a new cost-sharing cap and possible civil penalties. Some could shift the lost revenue into premiums charged to all enrollees [S3].
